sections.title: The library that lends more
sections.passage:
A. In 2018, the coastal town of Bellwick opened a library inside a former railway station. The project was called Open Doors. Architect Maya Patel kept the original clock above the entrance, but replaced the ticket windows with reading desks. The council paid for construction; a neighbourhood association supplied second-hand furniture. The building opens at nine in the morning, six days a week, and closes on Mondays.

B. Rather than buying every title immediately, the librarians first asked residents what they wanted to read. Gardening books were requested most often. A survey received 240 replies. A quiet room for independent study was created upstairs, while the ground floor includes a workshop and a children's corner. Large signs and a step-free entrance help visitors find their way. There are no café facilities inside the building.

C. The library lends tools as well as books. Members may borrow a drill for seven days, but must attend a safety demonstration first. Sewing machines can only be used in the workshop. The service is free for residents. Visitors from outside Bellwick pay a small annual membership fee. Staff record each loan electronically, although paper receipts are available on request.

D. An evaluation after the first year found that visits had doubled compared with the old library. However, the report did not measure changes in reading ability. Researcher Daniel Wu warned against assuming that attendance alone proves educational improvement. He recommended interviewing visitors again after three years. The council decided to maintain opening hours rather than extend them.

Building plan: entering from the south, the information desk is directly ahead. To the west of the desk is the workshop; to the east is the children's corner. Stairs behind the desk lead to the quiet room upstairs. The north door opens onto a garden.

sections.title: A living roof
sections.passage:
A. The Green Roof Project began at Northbridge College in 2020. Botanist Elena Ross wanted to discover whether planted roofs could reduce summer heat in small buildings. Her team compared two identical sheds, one with a planted roof and one with a bare metal roof. Both sheds faced south and neither contained air conditioning. Sensors measured the indoor temperature every fifteen minutes.

B. The researchers chose sedum because its thick leaves retain water. Beneath the plants lay eight centimetres of growing material, followed by a drainage mat and a waterproof membrane. Rainwater left the roof through an outlet on its eastern edge. The planted roof needed watering during the first month, but after that it relied on rainfall except during unusually dry weeks.

C. On the hottest afternoon, the shed with the planted roof was four degrees cooler. In winter, the temperature difference was smaller. The team recorded 18 species of insects on the roof, compared with five near the bare shed. These observations suggest a benefit for wildlife, but the researchers did not investigate birds or small mammals. No chemicals were applied to either roof.

D. Engineer Oliver Chen checked the structure before planting. Wet soil adds weight, so he reinforced two support beams. He argued that structural checks should precede any installation. Ross agreed but said maintenance costs also deserved attention. The project used volunteer labour for planting, while a grant covered sensors and materials.

E. The college plans to extend the study to a taller building. The current results cannot automatically be applied to every roof: wind and shade may change performance. Ross recommends local trials instead of a single national design. She has not claimed that green roofs can replace parks.

sections.title: Two wheels, different journeys
sections.passage:
A. A trial in the town of Alder Bay examined how people use shared bicycles. Transport analyst Luis Ahmed invited 120 adults to participate for six weeks. Half received access to ordinary bicycles, while the rest received electric bicycles. Participants logged their journeys in a diary. The study took place in spring, before the busiest tourist season.

B. Ordinary bicycles were used mainly for short journeys to shops. Electric bicycles were more often used for commuting up the steep road to the hospital. Average trip length was three kilometres for ordinary bicycles and seven for electric bicycles. Riders in both groups said secure parking was more useful than a mobile application with extra features.

C. There were three collection points: the station, the market and the hospital. The station offered 20 spaces and a repair stand. The market had 12 spaces but no repair equipment. The hospital had 16 spaces and a shelter. In the town map, the station is west of the river, the market east of the river, and the hospital north of the market. A footbridge connects the station and market.

D. Ahmed found that some participants replaced car journeys, but others replaced walking trips. Therefore the change in total emissions was uncertain. He said future studies should measure earlier travel habits before bicycles are supplied. Participant Nora Field enjoyed using an electric bicycle but worried about battery replacement costs. Participant Sam Ellis preferred an ordinary bicycle because it was easier to carry upstairs.

E. The town council agreed to continue the project for another year. The next stage will include winter travel and interviews with people who chose not to participate. Ahmed cautioned that the small volunteer sample might not represent every resident. Results from the trial were published on the council website in July.

Today our main exhibition is on the ground floor. It describes local fishing and boat building. Start in the east gallery, where you will find a restored wooden boat. sections.transcript: Demonstration audio. Part 3. Tutor: Tell me about your project, Mia. Student: We want to study food waste in student kitchens. We considered a questionnaire, but decided to use daily diaries instead. Tutor: How many participants? Student: Thirty volunteers from three halls of residence. Each will record discarded food for fourteen days. We will supply digital scales so they can measure its weight. Tutor: What categories will you use? Student: Fruit and vegetables, cooked meals, and bread. We will exclude liquids because measuring them consistently would be difficult. Tutor: What about privacy? Student: Diaries will use identification numbers, not names. We will store the files on the university server. Tutor: When is the pilot? Student: Next Monday, with four students. The final report is due in November. Tutor: Remember to discuss limitations. Volunteers might change their habits because they know they are being observed. Student: We will mention that in the conclusion.

sections.transcript: Demonstration audio. Part 4. Today we will examine the restoration of Brook Lane Stream. For decades it flowed through a concrete channel built to reduce flooding near factories. In 2015, the council began removing sections of concrete. Engineers widened the channel and created shallow banks. These banks were planted with native grasses. Instead of carrying water away as quickly as possible, the new design lets it spread into a meadow during heavy rain. The meadow normally serves as public open space. Biologist Sarah Dean monitored the project for five years. She measured water temperature every hour and counted aquatic insects each spring. Shade from new trees reduced the highest summer temperature by two degrees. The team found nine species of aquatic insects in the first year and seventeen in the fifth. However, water quality still declined after storms because polluted runoff entered from roads. Dean recommended filtering that runoff before it reaches the stream. The project cost two million pounds. Most funding came from a regional environment fund, with a smaller contribution from the council. Local volunteers now remove litter once a month.

sections.title: Learning a craft
sections.passage: When Lena Brooks moved to Westmere, she knew nobody in the town. She enrolled in an evening pottery course at the local college, hoping to meet people. The course lasted ten weeks and was taught by artist Peter Shaw. The first lesson focused on preparing clay, not using a wheel. Students kneaded it carefully to remove air bubbles, which can cause cracks during firing. Shaw encouraged beginners to make simple bowls before attempting narrow vases. Each student received two kilograms of clay per session. Tools were supplied, but students brought their own aprons. The workshop had six wheels shared by twelve students. Working in pairs gave learners time to watch each other and exchange suggestions. Lena found centring the clay particularly difficult. After practising, she discovered that steady pressure mattered more than speed. Finished pieces were left to dry for seven days before their first firing. Students then applied glaze with brushes. The kiln reached 1200 degrees during the final firing. Electricity costs were included in the course fee. At the final exhibition, visitors could buy students’ work; proceeds went to a local food bank. Lena sold three bowls. She later joined a cooperative studio, where members share both equipment and cleaning duties. She says the friendships have mattered as much as the objects she learned to make.

sections.title: A tour of question types
sections.passage:
A. In 2018, the coastal town of Bellwick opened a library inside a former railway station. The project was called Open Doors. Architect Maya Patel kept the original clock above the entrance, but replaced the ticket windows with reading desks. The council paid for construction; a neighbourhood association supplied second-hand furniture. The building opens at nine in the morning, six days a week, and closes on Mondays.

B. Rather than buying every title immediately, the librarians first asked residents what they wanted to read. Gardening books were requested most often. A survey received 240 replies. A quiet room for independent study was created upstairs, while the ground floor includes a workshop and a children's corner. Large signs and a step-free entrance help visitors find their way. There are no café facilities inside the building.

C. The library lends tools as well as books. Members may borrow a drill for seven days, but must attend a safety demonstration first. Sewing machines can only be used in the workshop. The service is free for residents. Visitors from outside Bellwick pay a small annual membership fee. Staff record each loan electronically, although paper receipts are available on request.

D. An evaluation after the first year found that visits had doubled compared with the old library. However, the report did not measure changes in reading ability. Researcher Daniel Wu warned against assuming that attendance alone proves educational improvement. He recommended interviewing visitors again after three years. The council decided to maintain opening hours rather than extend them.

Building plan: entering from the south, the information desk is directly ahead. To the west of the desk is the workshop; to the east is the children's corner. Stairs behind the desk lead to the quiet room upstairs. The north door opens onto a garden.

A. The Green Roof Project began at Northbridge College in 2020. Botanist Elena Ross wanted to discover whether planted roofs could reduce summer heat in small buildings. Her team compared two identical sheds, one with a planted roof and one with a bare metal roof. Both sheds faced south and neither contained air conditioning. Sensors measured the indoor temperature every fifteen minutes.

B. The researchers chose sedum because its thick leaves retain water. Beneath the plants lay eight centimetres of growing material, followed by a drainage mat and a waterproof membrane. Rainwater left the roof through an outlet on its eastern edge. The planted roof needed watering during the first month, but after that it relied on rainfall except during unusually dry weeks.

C. On the hottest afternoon, the shed with the planted roof was four degrees cooler. In winter, the temperature difference was smaller. The team recorded 18 species of insects on the roof, compared with five near the bare shed. These observations suggest a benefit for wildlife, but the researchers did not investigate birds or small mammals. No chemicals were applied to either roof.

D. Engineer Oliver Chen checked the structure before planting. Wet soil adds weight, so he reinforced two support beams. He argued that structural checks should precede any installation. Ross agreed but said maintenance costs also deserved attention. The project used volunteer labour for planting, while a grant covered sensors and materials.

E. The college plans to extend the study to a taller building. The current results cannot automatically be applied to every roof: wind and shade may change performance. Ross recommends local trials instead of a single national design. She has not claimed that green roofs can replace parks.

A. A trial in the town of Alder Bay examined how people use shared bicycles. Transport analyst Luis Ahmed invited 120 adults to participate for six weeks. Half received access to ordinary bicycles, while the rest received electric bicycles. Participants logged their journeys in a diary. The study took place in spring, before the busiest tourist season.

B. Ordinary bicycles were used mainly for short journeys to shops. Electric bicycles were more often used for commuting up the steep road to the hospital. Average trip length was three kilometres for ordinary bicycles and seven for electric bicycles. Riders in both groups said secure parking was more useful than a mobile application with extra features.

C. There were three collection points: the station, the market and the hospital. The station offered 20 spaces and a repair stand. The market had 12 spaces but no repair equipment. The hospital had 16 spaces and a shelter. In the town map, the station is west of the river, the market east of the river, and the hospital north of the market. A footbridge connects the station and market.

D. Ahmed found that some participants replaced car journeys, but others replaced walking trips. Therefore the change in total emissions was uncertain. He said future studies should measure earlier travel habits before bicycles are supplied. Participant Nora Field enjoyed using an electric bicycle but worried about battery replacement costs. Participant Sam Ellis preferred an ordinary bicycle because it was easier to carry upstairs.

E. The town council agreed to continue the project for another year. The next stage will include winter travel and interviews with people who chose not to participate. Ahmed cautioned that the small volunteer sample might not represent every resident. Results from the trial were published on the council website in July.

sections.transcript: Demonstration audio. Part 1. Welcome to the Riverside Garden registration desk. My name is Anna. Our garden is on Willow Street, next to the old post office. New members pay eighteen pounds for the season. The next introduction session is on Saturday at ten in the morning. Please bring gloves; we provide the tools. You can grow vegetables and flowers, but fruit trees are not permitted because their roots require too much space. Each plot measures six square metres. There is a water tap beside the wooden shed. Members must lock the main gate when they leave. To report a problem, email our coordinator, whose name is Martin. We hold our annual harvest picnic in September. The garden closes at sunset each evening.
